direct_answer: Fatigue is common in many types of arthritis, especially inflammatory arthritis. Inflammation, pain, poor sleep, low mood, anaemia and some medicines can contribute. Pacing, regular activity, good sleep habits and treating underlying causes can help. Talk to your GP or rheumatology team if fatigue is affecting your life.

content:
Arthritis fatigue is more than feeling a bit tired. Many people describe overwhelming exhaustion that does not go away with rest.

This guide explains common causes and practical ways to manage it. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

How it differs from ordinary tiredness

  • It can come on suddenly.
  • It is not always relieved by rest or sleep.
  • It can affect thinking and concentration.
  • It can vary from day to day.

Common contributing factors

  • Inflammation in inflammatory arthritis.
  • Pain and poor sleep.
  • Low mood or anxiety.
  • Anaemia or thyroid problems.
  • Some medicines.
  • Reduced fitness.

What helps

  • Pacing activities and planning rest breaks.
  • Regular, gentle physical activity.
  • A regular sleep routine.
  • Treating inflammation, pain or low mood.
  • Keeping a diary to spot patterns.

When to talk to your team

Tell your GP or rheumatology team if fatigue is new, getting worse or affecting daily life. They may check blood tests and review treatment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can exercise really help fatigue?

Regular, gradual activity can improve fatigue for many people.

Is fatigue a sign my arthritis is active?

It can be, especially in inflammatory arthritis. Tell your team.
